newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Trade in wheat contracts grows on Belgrade bourse.
newsitem.headline: Trade in wheat contracts grows on Belgrade bourse.

text.p: The Belgrade Stock Exchange (BSE) attracted growing interest in wheat contracts in January, boosting their share of its monthly turnover to 27 percent, BSE said as another two-month sale period expired on Friday.

In January BSE saw 28 transactions in wheat contracts totalling 37.494 million dinars ($6.88 million), sharply up on eight deals worth 4.274 million dinars in December. The December figure corresponded to four percent of BSE monthly turnover.
The bourse reported a total of 47,530 tonnes worth 48.177 million dinars sold since December 7, compared with 165,000 tonnes offered.
"This is very encouraging, not only in terms of volume but also when you look at numbers of investors," BSE commodities specialist Goran Altaras told Reuters.
Serbia's Commodity Reserve Agency relaunched forward wheat contracts last October to help finance advance purchases of up to 1.2 million tonnes of the 1997 crop.
Over the past four months it has offered a total of 330,000 tonnes of wheat, selling 84,690.
The contract's face value is 9,000 dinars, with 10 tonnes of wheat sold as collateral and a 32 percent discount. The paper also provides holders with an export licence.
Traders said low price and fears that Yugoslavia might not produce as much wheat as planned were the key reasons behind January's performance.
"It's a lucrative investment in terms of price. Wheat sells at 0.9 dinars per kilo and the same quantity already fetches 11.6-1.65 dinars on the spot market," a trader said.

Investors, mainly flour mills, were buying for their own needs and hedging against future price risk. Analysts said fears of a possible wheat shortage in 1997 had pushed mills to buy. "They want to be sure that 1996 will not repeat itself."
Yugoslavia's wheat output fell to a 25-year low of 1.72 million tonnes in 1996 after area had been reduced sharply. Output was also affected by bad weather and a lack of fuel and fertiliser.
"Nobody seems to believe official plans that Yugoslavia will produce enough wheat in 1997 and have around one million tonnes surplus for exports," an analyst said.
Altaras said, "They (flour mills) would have bought even more contracts if they had more money.
"It would be good to see banks on this market, but their liquidity is so poor and most of them have more urgent matters to attend to in order to avoid liquidation."
Commercial banks have appealed to the central bank to relax its tough reserve requirement regulations and allow them to hold half of the reserve requirement in wheat contracts, but without success.
But analysts said banks would have no interest to commit funds to a period as long as 285 days in a country shaken by 12 weeks of political crisis and economic chaos.

The Commodity Reserve Agency was expected to open the third round of wheat sales as early as next week in an attempt to secure more funds to finance the ailing agriculture sector, to which the Serbian government owes around 800 million dinars.
Serbia's 1997 budget envisages around 930 million dinars for agriculture, far less than the state devotes to the police, economists said.
Market analysts suggested a slightly bigger wheat discount could attract more buyers, but BSE officials expected no changes.
-- Gordana Filipoivic, Belgrade newsroom +381 11 222 4254
